topic: Theme 2: The UK Economy - Performance and Policies
subject: economics

items.title: The Soviet economy grew faster than the US for decades
items.claim: From the 1928 first Five-Year Plan to the late 1960s, how did Soviet growth compare to US growth?

options.text: The Soviet economy was always smaller and grew more slowly than the US
Soviet GDP growth averaged roughly 5-6% annually through the 1950s, faster than the US in the same period — before stagnating sharply in the 1970s-80s
Soviet GDP collapsed in 1932 and never recovered
The Soviet economy never produced reliable statistics

items.reveal:
CIA estimates put Soviet GDP growth at 5.7% (1950s) and 5.2% (1960s), against US rates of 3-4%. The growth was 'extensive' — pulling labour out of agriculture, building heavy industry, exploiting massive natural resources — rather than 'intensive' productivity gains.

By the 1970s the extensive sources were exhausted. Innovation faltered, oil propped up the system in the 1970s, then the 1980s collapse came when oil prices fell and reform under Gorbachev destabilised what remained.

Robert Allen, Stephen Kotkin and others have documented this trajectory in detail.
items.why: 'Communism never works' as a one-liner ignores 40 years of measurable, fast growth. The interesting question is why the model worked for extensive industrialisation but failed at the next stage.

items.title: Dutch disease named for Netherlands natural gas
items.claim: The 'Dutch disease' concept emerged from observing the Netherlands after its 1959 Groningen natural gas discovery. What's the mechanism?

options.text: Resource exports appreciate the real exchange rate, making non-resource tradable sectors (manufacturing) uncompetitive; when the resource is exhausted or prices fall, the diminished manufacturing base struggles to recover
Resource discovery always raises GDP permanently

items.reveal:
The Economist coined the term in 1977. Corden and Neary (1982) formalised the mechanism in a two-sector model with traded and non-traded goods.

Observed cases: Netherlands itself (1960s-70s); Venezuela's oil dependence; Nigeria; arguably the UK in the North Sea oil era. Counter-examples (Norway's sovereign wealth fund) show institutional design can mitigate the effect.

The broader 'resource curse' literature (Sachs and Warner, Acemoglu and others) extends to institutional and political channels.
items.why: Natural resource booms are mixed blessings. The institutional and macroeconomic management determines whether they fund long-run development or undermine it.

items.title: Almost no professional forecaster saw 2008 coming
items.claim: After the 2008 financial crisis, the Queen famously asked LSE economists why no one saw it coming. What's the accurate picture?

options.text: Most leading economists predicted the crisis from the early 2000s
A small number of analysts (Raghuram Rajan, Nouriel Roubini, Steve Keen, Brooksley Born, Michael Burry) warned about systemic risk; the consensus, including the IMF and most central banks, did not
The IMF published a precise prediction in 2006
The crisis was a complete surprise that no one anywhere foresaw

items.reveal:
Rajan's 2005 Jackson Hole paper ('Has Financial Development Made the World Riskier?') was dismissed by Larry Summers. Roubini was nicknamed 'Dr Doom' for warnings from 2006. Steve Keen had modelled private debt dynamics. Michael Burry famously bet against subprime (Big Short). The Bank for International Settlements raised flags.

Macroeconomic models in use (DSGE) had no banking sector and no default. The Queen's 2008 question to LSE got a follow-up letter (2009) from leading British economists admitting a 'failure of the collective imagination of many bright people... to understand the risks to the system as a whole.'
items.why: Economics' forecasting record isn't great — but the deeper issue was that mainstream models couldn't even represent the relevant risks. Heterodoxy isn't always wrong.
